大家好！

CIRCLE 1  A Personal Project

03  When a companion's service ends
当陪伴机器人的服务停止时
Target 1:03–2:16

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
A robot that talks with you can become a companion. Some robots depend on a company's servers for conversation. Those services need people and money to keep running, and sometimes they have to end. I saw sad news about robots that could no longer talk, even though they were still in people's homes. I wondered whether an open community could help people keep their robots going.

That idea became Stack-chan: a palm-sized, open-source robot with two motors and a simple face. Its slogan is “A communication robot in your hands.” That means both a robot small enough to hold, and the freedom to change it and help shape its future.

Looking back over these five years, I see a community growing in ever-widening circles, bringing Stack-chan into more people’s hands. Let's look at how these circles grew. The first circle began with my own making.

[END OF SPOKEN TEXT]

Around 2018, I shared face-animation software for M5Stack. I wanted to give that small face a moving body. After joining a robotics startup, I learned mechanical design, circuits, and embedded software. I tried those skills in my spare time and gradually built my own robot. The Moddable SDK is a set of tools for developing software for small devices in JavaScript. Because I already knew the language, it gave me a familiar way into embedded development. This personal project grew while I was learning.

slides.notesText:

05  The birth of Stack-chan
Stack-chan 的诞生
Target 2:59–3:45

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
This is the tweet where I shared a photo of Stack-chan in my hand. The name Stack-chan combines M5Stack with “chan,” an affectionate Japanese suffix. With a battery inside, it could move without a power cable. I wrote that it had become a real robot I could hold in the palm of my hand. The first version was rough, but that small face now had a moving body. This was before I knew what other people would make with it.

So I made another octopus.

[STAGE DIRECTION — DO NOT READ ALOUD]
[Let the second octopus register. Pause briefly, without waiting for laughter.]

The teacher still wasn't satisfied, and I felt sad. But I was attached to my simple octopus. That memory stays with me when I think about making robots. Complexity and attachment are different things. A simple creation can mean a lot to its maker. I want people to be able to show what they made with pride, even when it is small or unfinished. That feeling is part of why I made Stack-chan simple, and why I have kept it simple.

slides.title: 07  Two motors and a simple face
slides.notesText:
[SLIDE / TIMING — DO NOT READ]
07  Two motors and a simple face
两个电机，一张简单的脸
Target 5:06–6:00

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
I don't want robot making to be a privilege reserved for experts. Connect two motors to a microcontroller, give it a simple face, and you already have a robot. A small movement can make that face feel alive. It doesn't have to be complicated to become something you care about. While we welcome more advanced experiments, the two-motor version remains a starting point. People can learn by building and changing it, with help where they need it. Then other makers began adapting it to their own needs.

[END OF SPOKEN TEXT]

The second circle grew with other makers in Japan. What could you change with parts you already have?

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
M5Stack, a compact module with a screen, became popular among makers in Japan early on. I was already part of that community. Many skilled makers shared their projects and advice, and distributors such as Switch Science helped make the hardware available. Some became Stack-chan's first builders. The rough first version took effort to assemble. Their creations showed me possibilities I had missed, and their feedback helped me improve it. I am grateful for both.

As the original creator, I wanted the name to stay open across different hardware, including M5Stack's. The designs and code have their own licenses. Together, open licenses and clear rules let people plan their own creations, including products for sale when the conditions allow. They can contribute in a way they can keep going. Takao's kits are a good example.

The fifth circle is still growing, with room for what comes next.

[STAGE DIRECTION — DO NOT READ ALOUD]
[Turn from the diagram to the audience. Pause for 2 seconds after “I grew with them.”]

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
As the community grew, my role changed too: manuals, a trademark, guidelines, communication tools, and business cards. I learned to respond to what people needed. Growing Together means this too: the members grew, the community grew, and I grew with them.

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
That influence goes both ways. The community's creations give me ideas for what I want to make next. With so many different Stack-chans, wouldn't you like to see them chatting together as friends? I want to try several Stack-chans talking together, with a person listening and joining when something interests them. Which robot speaks next? Where does it look? How does it notice someone wants to join? Blinking, gaze, small movements, and pauses still matter, even with two motors. That's what I'd like to explore next.

slides.notesText:

22  Come and join us
欢迎你来参与
Target 17:46–18:52

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
Come and join us. I hope our community will grow to ten thousand people around the world, and I would love you to be part of it. What would you enjoy making? You can build your own robot or begin with an M5StackChan, then bring something you enjoy making. You can program, draw a comic, make an outfit, share a photo, or tell us where you got stuck. I want the community to be a safe base that welcomes experiments and mistakes. From there, we can go out and try our own adventures. You can make something ambitious, or enjoy a small two-motor robot at your own pace.

[STAGE DIRECTION — DO NOT READ ALOUD]
[Look toward the audience. Pause for 2 seconds after “the makers, the community, and me.”]

[READ ALOUD — ENGLISH]
We are growing together: the makers, the community, and me. Today, being here is my small adventure. Thank you.
